supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix nonnegative integers $n_0,n_1,n_2,n_3$ and ordered coordinate bases, and put $C^k:=\mathbb R^{n_k}$ for $k=0,1,2,3$. The dual space $(C^k)^*$ is the vector space of linear functionals $C^k\to\mathbb R$, with the dual basis to the chosen coordinate basis. Let $D_0\in\mathbb R^{n_1\times n_0}$, $D_1\in\mathbb R^{n_2\times n_1}$, and $D_2\in\mathbb R^{n_3\times n_2}$ be linear maps satisfying $D_1D_0=0$ and $D_2D_1=0$. This data is a finite cochain complex. The transpose $D_k^{\mathsf T}$ denotes the representing matrix of the dual linear map in the dual bases. Let $M_1\in\mathbb R^{n_1\times n_1}$ and $M_2\in\mathbb R^{n_2\times n_2}$ be symmetric positive-definite matrices: $v^{\mathsf T}M_kv>0$ for each nonzero $v\in C^k$. They represent linear maps $M_1:C^1\to(C^1)^*$ and $M_2:C^2\to(C^2)^*$ in the chosen bases; in positive dimensions their inverses exist by the finite-dimensional positive-matrix result cited below, and the unique map on a zero-dimensional space is its own inverse.

The finite state space is $\mathcal X:=C^2\oplus(C^1)^*$, with state $(b,d)$, where $b$ is a column of $C^2$ coordinates and $d$ is a column in the dual basis of $(C^1)^*$. In this item, “phase space” means this finite-dimensional state space only; no symplectic form is asserted. On an open interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$, a semidiscrete trajectory is a continuously differentiable map $t\mapsto(b(t),d(t))\in\mathcal X$ satisfying

$$\dot b(t)=-D_1M_1^{-1}d(t),\qquad \dot d(t)=D_1^{\mathsf T}M_2b(t).$$

Its two discrete constraints are $D_2b(t)=0$ in $C^3$ and $D_0^{\mathsf T}d(t)=0$ in $(C^0)^*$. The associated quadratic energy is

$$\mathcal E(b,d):=\tfrac12\left(b^{\mathsf T}M_2b+d^{\mathsf T}M_1^{-1}d\right).$$

All objects here are finite-dimensional real linear-algebra data. The term “Maxwell” names this algebraic model and does not identify it with a continuum Maxwell or Einstein–Maxwell solution.

They represent linear maps $M_1:C^1\to(C^1)^*$ and $M_2:C^2\to(C^2)^*$ in the chosen bases; in positive dimensions their inverses exist by the finite-dimensional positive-matrix result cited below, and the unique map on a zero-dimensional space is its own inverse.

The finite state space is $\mathcal X:=C^2\oplus(C^1)^*$, with state $(b,d)$, where $b$ is a column of $C^2$ coordinates and $d$ is a column in the dual basis of $(C^1)^*$. In this item, “phase space” means this finite-dimensional state space only; no symplectic form is asserted. On an open interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$, a semidiscrete trajectory is a continuously differentiable map $t\mapsto(b(t),d(t))\in\mathcal X$ satisfying

$$\dot b(t)=-D_1M_1^{-1}d(t),\qquad \dot d(t)=D_1^{\mathsf T}M_2b(t).$$

Its two discrete constraints are $D_2b(t)=0$ in $C^3$ and $D_0^{\mathsf T}d(t)=0$ in $(C^0)^*$. The associated quadratic energy is

$$\mathcal E(b,d):=\tfrac12\left(b^{\mathsf T}M_2b+d^{\mathsf T}M_1^{-1}d\right).$$

All objects here are finite-dimensional real linear-algebra data. The term “Maxwell” names this algebraic model and does not identify it with a continuum Maxwell or Einstein–Maxwell solution.

Use the finite cochain data fixed by the preceding definition item, namely finite real coordinate spaces $C^0,C^1,C^2,C^3$, maps $D_0,D_1,D_2$ with $D_1D_0=D_2D_1=0$, and symmetric positive-definite mass maps $M_1,M_2$. Inputs are rational matrices $D_0,D_1,D_2,M_1,M_2$, rational initial coordinates $b_0\in C^2$ and $d_{1/2}\in(C^1)^*$, a positive rational step size $\tau$, and an integer $N\geq0$. The matrices and states use the fixed ordered bases and dual bases from that definition. All arithmetic is exact over $\mathbb Q$; floating-point arithmetic is not part of this algorithm.

First compute $R=M_1^{-1}$ once by fixed-order, no-row-swap Gauss–Jordan elimination of the augmented matrix $[M_1\mid I_{n_1}]$. For each pivot column $j=1,\ldots,n_1$, let $p$ be the current entry in position $(j,j)$. If $p=0$, return an inconsistency error. Otherwise divide row $j$ by $p$ and, for every $k\neq j$, replace row $k$ by row $k$ minus its current column-$j$ entry times row $j$. After all columns are processed, let $R$ be the right block. For $n_1=0$, take the unique empty matrix for $R$ and perform no elimination.

Set $(b,d):=(b_0,d_{1/2})$ and record this initial state. For each $n=0,\ldots,N-1$, in the stated order compute

$$b_{\mathrm{new}}:=b-\tau D_1Rd,\qquad d_{\mathrm{new}}:=d+\tau D_1^{\mathsf T}M_2b_{\mathrm{new}}.$$

Append $(b_{\mathrm{new}},d_{\mathrm{new}})$ to the output list and then set $(b,d):=(b_{\mathrm{new}},d_{\mathrm{new}})$. The output consists of the $N+1$ states $(b_n,d_{n+1/2})$ for $0\leq n\leq N$. The error branch is unreachable on admissible inputs; the separate finite-step termination lemma proves this and the exact inverse output.

derivations.claim:
For one update, the complex identities give
$D_2b_{n+1}=D_2b_n-\tau D_2D_1M_1^{-1}d_{n+1/2}=D_2b_n$ and
$D_0^{\mathsf T}d_{n+3/2}=D_0^{\mathsf T}d_{n+1/2}+\tau(D_1D_0)^{\mathsf T}M_2b_{n+1}=D_0^{\mathsf T}d_{n+1/2}$.
Thus both constraints are preserved, with no restriction on $\tau$.

For a semidiscrete solution, symmetry of $M_2$ and $M_1^{-1}$ gives
$\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal E=\dot b^{\mathsf T}M_2b+\dot d^{\mathsf T}M_1^{-1}d
=-d^{\mathsf T}M_1^{-1}D_1^{\mathsf T}M_2b+d^{\mathsf T}M_1^{-1}D_1^{\mathsf T}M_2b=0$.
Therefore $\mathcal E$ is constant on the solution interval.

In positive dimensions set $x_n=M_2^{1/2}b_n$, $y_{n+1/2}=M_1^{-1/2}d_{n+1/2}$, and $S=M_2^{1/2}D_1M_1^{-1/2}$. By [F3], the update becomes $x_{n+1}=x_n-\tau Sy_{n+1/2}$ and $y_{n+3/2}=y_{n+1/2}+\tau S^{\mathsf T}x_{n+1}$. Write $x=x_n$, $y=y_{n+1/2}$, and $x'=x_{n+1}=x-\tau Sy$. Then
$\lVert y+\tau S^{\mathsf T}x'\rVert_2^2
=\lVert y\rVert_2^2+2\tau x'^{\mathsf T}Sy+\tau^2\lVert S^{\mathsf T}x'\rVert_2^2$
and
$-\tau x'^{\mathsf T}S(y+\tau S^{\mathsf T}x')
=-\tau x'^{\mathsf T}Sy-\tau^2\lVert S^{\mathsf T}x'\rVert_2^2$.
Adding these to $\lVert x'\rVert_2^2$ cancels the squared terms and leaves $\lVert x'\rVert_2^2+\lVert y\rVert_2^2+\tau x'^{\mathsf T}Sy$. Finally,
$\lVert x'\rVert_2^2+\tau x'^{\mathsf T}Sy
=\lVert x-\tau Sy\rVert_2^2+\tau(x-\tau Sy)^{\mathsf T}Sy
=\lVert x\rVert_2^2-\tau x^{\mathsf T}Sy$,
so $Q_{n+1}=Q_n$. If either coordinate space is zero-dimensional, the cross term vanishes and the update leaves the squared Euclidean norm on the remaining state space unchanged.

By [F4] and [F5],
$|x^{\mathsf T}Sy|\leq\lVert x\rVert_2\lVert Sy\rVert_2\leq\sigma\lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2
\leq\frac{\sigma}{2}(\lVert x\rVert_2^2+\lVert y\rVert_2^2)$.
Hence $Q_n\geq(1-\tau\sigma/2)(\lVert x_n\rVert_2^2+\lVert y_{n+1/2}\rVert_2^2)$, which is strictly positive for every nonzero state when $\tau\sigma<2$. If $\sigma=0$ or a coordinate space is zero, the cross term vanishes and the same conclusion holds for every $\tau>0$.

derivations.claim: If $n_1>0$, the initial trailing block $S_1=M_1$ is symmetric positive definite by [F1]. After eliminating the first $j-1$ columns without row swaps, the left augmented block has form $\begin{pmatrix}I_{j-1}&A\\0&S_j\end{pmatrix}$, where $S_j$ is the remaining Schur complement. Write $S_j=\begin{pmatrix}p&r^{\mathsf T}\\r&C\end{pmatrix}$. Since $S_j$ is positive definite, $p>0$, so the prescribed diagonal pivot is nonzero. The row operations in column $j$ replace the remaining block by $S_{j+1}=C-rp^{-1}r^{\mathsf T}$. For any nonzero $y$, put $x=-p^{-1}r^{\mathsf T}y$; then $(x,y)\neq0$ and $y^{\mathsf T}S_{j+1}y=(x,y)^{\mathsf T}S_j(x,y)>0$. Hence $S_{j+1}$ is positive definite. Induction proves that every no-row-swap pivot is positive and the error branch is unreachable. Each row operation is invertible; after the last column the left block is the identity, so the right block is exactly $M_1^{-1}$. For $n_1=0$, the inverse is the unique empty matrix and there are no pivot steps.

The input entries are rational. Each row operation uses addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division by a nonzero rational pivot from step 1.1, so every intermediate entry and the final inverse remain rational. The elimination loop has exactly $n_1$ finite iterations; consequently it terminates with an exact rational output.

Dense no-row-swap Gauss–Jordan elimination performs $O(n_1^2)$ row-entry updates per pivot column and hence $O(n_1^3)$ arithmetic operations. Each evolution step uses matrix-vector products with costs $O(n_1^2)$ for $M_1^{-1}d$, $O(n_1n_2)$ for each multiplication by $D_1$ or $D_1^{\mathsf T}$, and $O(n_2^2)$ for $M_2b$. There are exactly $N$ such steps. The matrices $D_0,D_1,D_2,M_1,M_2$ have respectively $n_1n_0,n_1n_2,n_3n_2,n_1^2,n_2^2$ entries; the inverse adds $n_1^2$, and the $N+1$ states add $(N+1)(n_1+n_2)$ entries. Their total is bounded by the stated storage order. When $N=0$, the initial state is returned without an update; when $n_1=0$ or $n_2=0$, the corresponding empty products and loops are finite and the same bounds remain valid. No bit-size or floating-point estimate follows from an arithmetic-operation count.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix nonnegative integers $n_0,n_1,n_2,n_3$ and ordered coordinate bases, and put $C^k:=\mathbb R^{n_k}$ for $k=0,1,2,3$. The dual space $(C^k)^*$ is the vector space of linear functionals $C^k\to\mathbb R$, with the dual basis to the chosen coordinate basis. Let $D_0\in\mathbb R^{n_1\times n_0}$, $D_1\in\mathbb R^{n_2\times n_1}$, and $D_2\in\mathbb R^{n_3\times n_2}$ be linear maps satisfying $D_1D_0=0$ and $D_2D_1=0$. This data is a finite cochain complex. The transpose $D_k^{\mathsf T}$ denotes the representing matrix of the dual linear map in the dual bases. Let $M_1\in\mathbb R^{n_1\times n_1}$ and $M_2\in\mathbb R^{n_2\times n_2}$ be symmetric positive-definite matrices: $v^{\mathsf T}M_kv>0$ for each nonzero $v\in C^k$. They represent linear maps $M_1:C^1\to(C^1)^*$ and $M_2:C^2\to(C^2)^*$ in the chosen bases; in positive dimensions their inverses exist by the finite-dimensional positive-matrix result cited below, and the unique map on a zero-dimensional space is its own inverse.

The finite state space is $\mathcal X:=C^2\oplus(C^1)^*$, with state $(b,d)$, where $b$ is a column of $C^2$ coordinates and $d$ is a column in the dual basis of $(C^1)^*$. In this item, “phase space” means this finite-dimensional state space only; no symplectic form is asserted. On an open interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$, a semidiscrete trajectory is a continuously differentiable map $t\mapsto(b(t),d(t))\in\mathcal X$ satisfying

$$\dot b(t)=-D_1M_1^{-1}d(t),\qquad \dot d(t)=D_1^{\mathsf T}M_2b(t).$$

Its two discrete constraints are $D_2b(t)=0$ in $C^3$ and $D_0^{\mathsf T}d(t)=0$ in $(C^0)^*$. The associated quadratic energy is

$$\mathcal E(b,d):=\tfrac12\left(b^{\mathsf T}M_2b+d^{\mathsf T}M_1^{-1}d\right).$$

All objects here are finite-dimensional real linear-algebra data. The term “Maxwell” names this algebraic model and does not identify it with a continuum Maxwell or Einstein–Maxwell solution.

Use the finite cochain data and exact update specified in the definition and algorithm items cited immediately below, with step size $\tau>0$. Every update preserves both constraints $D_2b=0$ and $D_0^{\mathsf T}d=0$. Every continuously differentiable semidiscrete solution conserves $\mathcal E(b,d)$. For the staggered sequence, define

$$Q_n:=b_n^{\mathsf T}M_2b_n+d_{n+1/2}^{\mathsf T}M_1^{-1}d_{n+1/2}-\tau b_n^{\mathsf T}M_2D_1M_1^{-1}d_{n+1/2}.$$

derivations.claim: The matrices in [A1] are the signed boundary-incidence maps of one oriented tetrahedron, with edges ordered $01,02,03,12,13,23$, faces ordered $012,013,023,123$, and cell orientation $0123$. Matrix multiplication gives $D_1D_0=0_{4\times4}$ and $D_2D_1=0_{1\times6}$. Also $D_2x=-1+1=0$ and $D_0^{\mathsf T}d_{1/2}=0_{4\times1}$, so the initial state satisfies both constraints.

Put $c:=(-1,1,-1,1)^{\mathsf T}$, so $D_2=c^{\mathsf T}$. Direct multiplication gives
$$D_1D_1^{\mathsf T}=\begin{pmatrix}3&1&-1&1\\1&3&1&-1\\-1&1&3&1\\1&-1&1&3\end{pmatrix}=4I_4-cc^{\mathsf T}.$$
For every $z\in\mathbb R^4$, this gives $\lVert D_1^{\mathsf T}z\rVert_2^2=4\lVert z\rVert_2^2-(c^{\mathsf T}z)^2\leq4\lVert z\rVert_2^2$. Hence, by Cauchy–Schwarz, $\lVert D_1v\rVert_2=\max_{\lVert z\rVert_2=1}|z^{\mathsf T}D_1v|\leq2\lVert v\rVert_2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^6$. Since $c^{\mathsf T}x=0$, $e:=x/\sqrt2$ is unit and $D_1D_1^{\mathsf T}e=4e$; consequently $f:=D_1^{\mathsf T}e/2$ is unit and $D_1f=2e$. Thus the operator norm of $D_1$ is exactly $2$, attained at $f$. Here $M_1=M_2=I$, so the $\sigma$ defined in [F3] is $2$. For a state $b=ue$, $d=vf$, the update in [F2] with $\tau=2$ gives $u^+=u-4v$ and $v^+=v+4u^+=4u-15v$, hence the invariant two-dimensional subspace has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&-4\\4&-15\end{pmatrix}$. The initial state has modal coordinates $(u,v)=(\sqrt2,0)$.

The matrix in step 2.1 has trace $-14$, determinant $1$, and eigenvalues $\lambda_-=-7-4\sqrt3$ and $\lambda_+=-7+4\sqrt3$, found by solving $\lambda^2+14\lambda+1=0$. Since $6<4\sqrt3<7$, $\lambda_-<-1$ and $-1<\lambda_+<0$. Direct substitution gives eigenvectors $v_-=(1,2+\sqrt3)^{\mathsf T}$ and $v_+=(1,2-\sqrt3)^{\mathsf T}$; their determinant is $-2\sqrt3\neq0$, so write the initial modal vector as $(\sqrt2,0)^{\mathsf T}=a v_-+b v_+$. The coefficient $a$ is nonzero, since otherwise $(\sqrt2,0)^{\mathsf T}$ would be a multiple of $v_+$, whose second coordinate $2-\sqrt3$ is nonzero. The first modal coordinate after $n$ steps is therefore $u_n=a\lambda_-^n+b\lambda_+^n$. If $u_n$ were bounded, then $b\lambda_+^n$ would be bounded because $|\lambda_+|<1$, so their difference $a\lambda_-^n$ would be bounded, contradicting $a\neq0$ and $|\lambda_-|>1$. Since $\lVert b_n\rVert_2\geq|u_n|$, the state orbit is unbounded.

By [F3], each update preserves both constraints, and step 1.1 sets them to zero initially. Explicitly, $D_2b^+=D_2b-\tau D_2D_1M_1^{-1}d=D_2b$ and $D_0^{\mathsf T}d^+=D_0^{\mathsf T}d+\tau(D_1D_0)^{\mathsf T}M_2b^+=D_0^{\mathsf T}d$, so induction gives zero constraints at every iterate. Thus exact constraint preservation holds at every step although this rational finite-complex algorithm has an unbounded orbit for $\tau\sigma=4>2$. This refutes the stated bounded-orbit claim.
